To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(a) iron-related proteins (IRP) in urine can be used as a biomarker for the diagnosis and monitoring of renal disease in HIV-infected children; (b) IRP in urine can be measured using a novel and rapid assay that is simple to perform; (c) IRP levels in urine are elevated in children with HIV-associated renal disease and correlate with the severity of the disease; (d) IRP levels are significantly higher in children with nephrotic range proteinuria
iron-related proteins are potential biomarkers for HIV-associated renal diseases in children.
The use of the urine biomarkers, including iron-related proteins (IRP) and kidney injury molecule-1, may be a useful tool for the early diagnosis of kidney injury in children with HIV infection.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the study of the structure and properties of iron-containing proteins.
the study of the mechanisms of iron homeostasis in health and disease, and with the identification of novel biomarkers for the diagnosis of iron overload and iron deficiency.
the identification of iron-related proteins in the urine of HIV-infected children with renal disease and the evaluation of their potential as biomarkers of kidney damage.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that

the use of the term "HIV-associated nephropathy" (HIVAN) is not recommended, as the term does not accurately describe the renal diseases in children with HIV infection, which are heterogeneous in nature and etiology.
iron-related proteins are candidate biomarkers of renal diseases in HIV-infected children.
there is a strong association between the presence of iron-related proteins and HIV-associated renal diseases in children.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
iron-related proteins are potential urine biomarkers for renal diseases in HIV-infected children.
we have identified a number of candidate biomarkers in the urine of HIV-infected children that may have utility in the diagnosis of renal diseases in this population.
iron is a major factor in renal disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the urine proteome can be used to identify biomarkers of HIV- and ART-related renal diseases.
the urine proteomic signature in HIV-infected children with renal diseases is different from that observed in HIV-uninfected children with renal disease.
